newsitem.title: UK: Bosnia talks link aid to war criminals, peace.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia talks link aid to war criminals, peace.

text.p: Major powers were set to end a two-day peace conference on Thursday by telling Bosnia's ethnic leaders they must fully implement a year-old peace pact and issue arrest warrants for war criminals or forfeit Western aid.

"The council's willingness to devote human and financial resources is dependent on a strengthened commitment from the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to implementation of the peace agreement," said a draft document obtained by Reuters.
The conference, attended by more than 50 nations, was also set to tell the leaders of the former Yugoslavia they must round up indicted war criminals if they wanted more aid.
The document urged that "the authorities concerned execute arrest warrants against indictees and surrender them to the (Hague war crimes) tribunal without further delay."

The conference was called to assess the state of peace one year after the fighting stopped. Frustration over repeated delays in implementing the civilian aspects of the so-called Dayton agreement has led Western leaders to link aid to a renewed commitment to genuine peace on the ground.
"These objectives require the full commitment of all the leaders of Bosnia and Herzegovina," according to the draft.

"The council is gravely concerned that the Council of Ministers (in Bosnia) has not yet been formed. Unless it is established the donor community will be reluctant to consider firm pledges of support for reconstruction in 1997.
A donor conference planned for February 1997 will therefore be at risk."
A similar conference to this week's talks would be called late next year to assess progress, it said.
This week's conference -- due to end later on Thursday -- spelt out what steps must be taken in the months ahead.
The draft welcomed "substantial progress made in the past year", saying peace had taken root, elections had been held and that reconstruction was underway.
"The next stage is to build upon the achievements of the past 12 months," it addded. "There are important areas of the peace agreement where little progress has been made."
Among the most contentious issues is the fate of suspected war criminals.

The vast majority of the 75 people indicted by a special tribunal at the Hague remain at large. Only five are held in jail and the most notorious -- former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his former army chief Ratko Mladic -- are free and believed to be pulling strings behind the scenes.
Delegates and ministers agreed to inject extra resources into the tribunal to improve its investigative capacity and insist on full cooperation with its investigations.

On other key points hammered out at Dayton, the draft document approved a "detailed and specific action programme" covering regional stabilisation, human rights, democratisation, displaced persons, freedom of movement, local elections, policing, market economy and reconstruction.
It also laid the groundwork for settling the problems of the central bank, mine removal, reconciliation, media, education, the strategic city of Brcko in northern Bosnia, and customs.
On the unresolved matter of freedom of movement -- a cornerstone of Dayton -- the document called for the elimination of laws and regulations that inhibit unrestricted passage.
